utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We're continuing with the Prosecution -- oh, cross-examination by Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Lazarevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. We will be continuing with our cross-examination where we left off yesterday. If you remember, we were looking at some photographs of the SUP building in Bosanski Samac, and now I would like, very briefly, in two or three questions, clear up some things. I understand fully that it is very hard for you to think back about all those events, but I think that we need to clarify the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the usher with the photograph F53. It's Exhibit P14 and the photograph number is 53.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please wait for the end of the interpretation before continuing on in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm specifically interested in the upper right-hand corner of this building. Do you see that window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what is this room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: This room that I'm indicating right now is the room of the communications centre, where the communications centre was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one more question pertaining to this photograph. On the ground floor, the second window from the door, with the bars, can you please tell me -- yes, that's the one- what room was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a room where the cell was, and I remember quite clearly that I was in that cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that the witness pointed a window on the upper right corner of the house, indicating that this is a communications centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And the second window, looking from the door, on the right side, and he -- indicating that this is a space where the cell where he was incarcerated was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now I would just like the assistance in showing the photograph F52. I don't need this photograph any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if I understood you correctly, according to what you indicated, this was the room where the cells were, but this photograph was taken inside the building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, this table -- this desk was not here, this chair was not here, and the wall here was not the way it is now. It was all covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but at any rate, this is the area, but of course the furniture -- I assume that it was the way you describe it. But what I wanted to know is whether this is that room or not. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this respect, I'm only interested in one more thing and then we will move on to another topic. There are two cells here; is that correct, or rather, you can see for yourself that there are two doors here, which would mean that there are two cells, one next to the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this room is located on the ground floor of the SUP building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Across the corridor from the doors to these cells there is nothing; there is only the wall. There are no rooms that one could enter from that part. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing there. This is the wall that divided the cells from the toilet, but one could not enter from this room but from another room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will ask you one more question in this regard. This is the only room in the SUP building where the cells were. There are no cells on the first floor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any. While I was there, there weren't any. I didn't go to any other cells, apart from these ones here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, I don't know what the situation was before or afterwards. I'm interested in the period while you were there, and from your statement, one could see that you were also upstairs in Dragan Lukac's office. Can you please tell me: Were there any cells, any room with cells on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lazarevic. I'd like to ask Witness A: Looking at the photograph, what is on the immediate left-hand side of the photograph, to the left of the numbers 1, 3? Is it a wall, another cell perhaps, a doorway? I'd like to have some sense of, if I was standing here, what I would be looking at. I hope the question is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Do you want me to clarify all this issue with the witness? Or maybe he can answer straight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can give you my answer immediately. I don't know what was here indicated with numbers 1, 3, but I don't know that this cell, it's a room. As you can see, this is not a big room. And as you entered it, to the left there was one door. This is one door to one of the cells, and this is the other door. Here it's leaning against the window that's looking out into the yard. That's the other cell. So this room here, it was divided in half, here up to the window, and to the right there was the wall, and here there was the entrance. And all this that I'm indicating now was made of some kind of steel, and it was painted this kind of a drab colour, SMB colour. Up here you can see the bars. So you can see, this is the first door, this is the other door, the first cell, the other cell. In my time, two people were here, and I was in the other cell with another prisoner. So when you opened -- when they closed this, we were unable to open it from the inside. We only got air through here and we could only look out at the wall. In fact, they could only look out at the wall, while we could look out through the window, if they allowed us, and if somebody opened the door, we were able to see, more or less, and recognise a person, if they allowed us or if we dared to look out. So this is a small room, quite small room, but it was also divided in two. This was made of iron or steel, and this wall here was all covered in blood and dirty, because I assume that other people had been imprisoned here before. There was this floor. And we had some kind of benches to sit on. And this is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could clarify even more. If you look at the photograph, on the right side you see a door handle. So this is taken from some sort of corridor, and the door was open. So the doors are on this side, so when they closed the door, that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I don't need this any more. And may the record reflect that the witness identified the cell where he was incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now I would like to move on to the topic of your meeting Mr. Zaric in the SUP building. You spoke about that here before this Trial Chamber. You said that you had gone to Milos Savic and that you heard Simo Zaric, that you had asked Milos Savic to take you to Simo Zaric to talk to him. I would like to clarify a few details regarding this conversation. When you spoke to Mr. Zaric, Milos Savic was also present there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, Savic got out and you were on your own with Simo Zaric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether on that occasion, when you were there with Mr. Zaric, that he said that nationalist parties were responsible for all that was happening at the time? Do you perhaps remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric did not blame you for anything in the course of that conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was quite angry. He was quite angry also with me. But he was angry in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, he didn't tell you, "You are responsible, you are guilty of this and that, you had this or you did that," he didn't blame you for anything, you personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, with regard to that conversation, whether Zaric said that he knew that Sulejman Tihic would be treated as a political prisoner, together with Izet Izetbegovic, Dragan Lukac, and he also mentioned your name, and he said that he hoped that you would be released quite soon. Was anything said to that effect at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to that effect, not in that sense. When I spoke to Mr. Zaric, I asked him, "Well, what is this? What's happening? You've seen what I look like. What am I guilty of? If I were guilty of anything, I wouldn't stay here in Samac; I would have gone somewhere." And then I told him, "Don't put me in the same position or the same situation as Mr. Tihic. Tihic was the president of the party." I didn't belong to any party. I was there as a reserve officer of the MUP, of the legal police force of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, sir. I didn't mean to interrupt your answer. Please do not misunderstand me. This is word for word what you already stated here. We already have that on record. I wanted to speed things up and to obtain all the facts that we need while respecting your time. This is precisely what you stated already here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just correct you. In that conversation, Lukac or Izetbegovic were not mentioned at all in that conversation. At that time I had no contact -- I had had no contact with Lukac or with Izetbegovic. I hadn't seen Izetbegovic at all. I was brought into the office and beaten together with Mr. Tihic, and that's when Simo told me, "You will be exchanged, you and Tihic will be exchanged as political prisoners." Now, if I have to explain to the Trial Chamber how the conversation went on, that he got down and then went back, if that's necessary, I will clarify all that and I will explain, but if it's not necessary ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if my learned colleague from the Prosecution thinks that he needs to obtain some other details regarding to this issue, he will do so in the re-direct. I have to say that I understood quite clearly what you just said, and I don't think it's necessary to clarify this any further. I'm interested in another thing, though. In that conversation with Mr. Zaric, when you spoke about that, you said that he wore a camouflage uniform and that he had a white band on his shoulder board. Do you remember that you said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it quite clearly. He wore a uniform, the uniform that we call a camouflage uniform. Some people call it a multicoloured uniform, but it's a camouflage uniform. He had a satchel with him, a leather satchel. He had a Scorpion, and now I don't remember whether it was on the left or right shoulder, but he had a white band that was tied to the upper part of the uniform. But I think -- I rather think it was the left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 8th, 9th, and 10th of October, and the 6th of December, 1994, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal in The Hague, a Mrs. Nancy Paterson, who worked in the OTP. She was in charge of this case, and to Mrs. Maria Velikonja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an official statement that was given to the investigators in the presence of the Prosecutors of the Tribunal in The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who was there, but I don't know the exact capacity in which they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave the statement, you gave it voluntarily, of your own free will; it was your decision to do so. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one exerted any kind of pressure on you for you to make the statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And no one influenced you in regard of the contents of the statement, in other words, so that you state something that -- that something was stated that you didn't actually say or something like that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You signed that statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before signing it, you familiarised yourself with the contents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, when you gave that statement, can we agree that your recollection of the events in April 1992 and onwards was better than it is now, in year 2002, ten years later? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, regarding some things, perhaps yes, but the things that affect me, the conversations and the suffering, I think I will remember that for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you a detail regarding the statement, and it pertains precisely to the conversation with Simo Zaric in the SUP building. It's on page 11 of your statement. Since we're talking about only a few sentences, I think that the simplest thing would be for me to read it to you, to quote from the statement. My colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor will make sure that what I'm reading is exactly the way it is written. The ERN number of this page is 00637838, and it says the following, pertaining to the conversation of Mr. Zaric -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection. I'm just trying to follow the evidence. I wonder if my learned friend knows where in the English statement it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that I don't have the English version here. I just have a B/C/S version. And my colleague would look at it in a second and they will inform the Prosecution in one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lazarevic. You could just give us the paragraph number, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Actually, in this statement, there are no paragraph numbers. So, this is a statement that was given in 1994. This is not his statement according to Rule 92 bis. It's on page 12 -- sorry. It's page 11, and it starts with "three or four times during the night ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, the Prosecutor now has it in front of him, and there's a statement that I noticed -- a sentence that I noticed here in your statement, and it goes as follows, regarding your conversation with Mr. Zaric: "I asked him what was going to happen with us, would they have to exchange us." So you told us here that Mr. Zaric told us that you would be exchanged, but in your statement it comes across that you, in fact, were the one who asked Mr. Zaric whether you should be exchanged. So, what is true? Is it true what it says here in your statement from 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember asking him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you allow for the possibility that it was that way, that it was you, in fact, who asked him whether you would be exchanged and asked him what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be, because I insisted, I asked to see Simo Zaric, because I thought that he was the only one able to help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have just one more question regarding this. During that conversation, did Zaric tell you that he was unable to prevent you being beaten? Do you remember him telling you that? Do you remember that detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now I'm going back to that same statement of yours from 1994, and the following paragraph. The Prosecutor should have it in front of him. You say that Mr. Zaric said that, "We would be exchanged soon, that he was unable to prevent us being beaten." So, this is what it says in your statement from 1994. Do you remember that? Do you remember that Mr. Zaric said something like that, that he was not able to prevent you from being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. I just told you that it could be so because I was the one who asked to see him. He saw what condition I was in, and the only thing I cared about was saving myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I have identical information regarding your condition from Mr. Zaric. He did tell me that you were in a very bad shape, so it is quite possible that you can't remember every single detail. Now, I would like to turn to the time when you were transferred to Brcko. You, naturally, were not the only one who was transferred to Brcko; there were other prisoners there with you. And bearing in mind the fact that you were in a very bad shape, I'm going to ask you whether you can confirm for me the fact that this transfer of yours to Brcko took place on the 26th of April, 1992, on the very same day when, in the courtyard of the TO building, Dikan was killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what date it was exactly when we were transferred to Brcko. All I know is that two or three days later, approximately, was the 1st of May, and I know that we were in Brcko on the 1st of May. I saw with my own eyes Lugar beating Dikan, and allegedly he was killed later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you: So did that take place on the same day? You were transferred in the evening hours on that same day, when you saw Lugar beating Dikan? Naturally, you can only state what you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, because I was loaded on the truck from the MUP building, together with several other people, whereas the others were collected at the headquarters building. I was taken from the MUP building to the headquarters building and then back to MUP. They did what they wanted, so that finally we were all disoriented. But I know for a fact that I was finally loaded onto the truck from the MUP building. I was in such bad shape that I was unable to climb onto the truck. The others had to lift me up. It was somewhat dark at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, some details that I discussed with Mr. Zaric and that have to do with that are somewhat different from your account. They're not very material details, but, however, Mr. Zaric told me that when he had entered the TO courtyard, he was together with Savo Cancarevic and Mihaljo and Topolovac and that Topolovac had read out the names from the list and that you were behind the doors, inside the TO building, almost unconscious, and that others were trying to assist you. Allegedly, even Mr. Zaric approached you behind that door. You asked him for water. So could it possibly be that this is how it was, bearing in mind that you were in a very bad shape? Mr. Zaric, in fact, even told me that he hardly recognised you upon seeing you. Did it perhaps happen in the way that I just described to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was imprisoned, I unfortunately was somebody who was most mistreated physically, and on several occasions I was even unconscious about my whereabouts. I know that people had to feed me. Some people gave me water, some people had to throw water over me, but I don't know who these people were. All I can confirm is that when we were boarded on the truck, Mr. Zaric was present, as was Topolovac and Cancarevic. He was probably in a better position to see what was happening there than I was, because my eyes were almost completely closed at the time. I could only hear things, but I couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know, this is what Mr. Zaric told me, that your condition was incredible, that you were basically unable to open your eyes. I would like to ask you now what is your opinion regarding this transfer to Brcko. Do you think that that was done at the insistence and organisation of Mr. Zaric -- MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, I mean, the question can only lead to speculation. This witness was barely conscious. How can he comment on the motives behind the transfer, whether it was done at the insistence or organisation of Mr. Zaric? Furthermore, it invites his opinion, and that's again just not necessary, unless this witness has got some direct insight into what motivated the transfer, something he heard or saw or has been told, then of course I have no objection. But the way the question is started to be phrased, it seems to me that we're going straight into some sort of invitation to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking for personal opinion in this respect. Of course, I can rephrase this question in some other way. I was just trying to simplify about his opinion and what he feels about that now, but I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this way: It is not disputed at all that you were in a critical condition while you were in the TO building and when you were transferred to Brcko. I'm interested in the following: Have you talked to somebody about this transfer to Brcko and how it came about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on things that I have learned, and in accordance with my opinion, we were transferred to Brcko because they wanted to transfer us from Samac because of those Serbs from Serbia who mistreated us the most. This is what we learned later on in Brcko. The other version, the other rumour, was that we had been transferred because other people had been arrested and they had nowhere to take them to. But my personal opinion is that the first version is more probable, that they wanted to save us from those Serbs from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, we will cover, in brief, your stay in Brcko. You told us what it was like there. Do you remember that upon your arrival to Brcko, Mr. Zaric came the very next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again that I was brought to Brcko in such a serious condition. Everybody had plastic handcuffs on them. I was the one without handcuffs. When we got there, they lined us up, and all I could see was some light, a little bit of light. My name was called out and I was immediately taken to another room. After that, Sulejman Tihic and Dragan Lukac were brought there as well. Now, was it the following day or the day after that, I can't tell you for sure. All I know is that Mr. Zaric visited us in that room. I couldn't see him very well, but I could hear him. He was accompanied by another person called Captain Petrovic. He was the security officer with the former JNA, and I remember Lukac asking me whether I knew who that person was. He referred to Petrovic. I replied to him that I didn't but that I had heard of him. One of them -- I don't remember whom -- said he should be taken to see the doctor. I truly don't remember who said that. All I know is that no doctor ever came to see me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody beat you in Brcko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meals were more regular than while in the TO building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received it more regularly; however, I couldn't eat, others had to feed me. But I guess one could say that it was better than in the TO building in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of those relatively better conditions, you were able to recover somewhat and get on your feet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a little bit better there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you happen to hear later on that Zaric was the one who initiated your transfer to Brcko? I realise that you were unable to know that at the time, but did you happen to hear this later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen. I don't know who initiated that. It is possible that he did it. If he had influence there, then it is likely. I don't know who was behind it, but whoever did it, I want to personally thank that person, both on my own behalf and on behalf of everybody else who survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to turn to some details that have to do with the day of exchange, but also some things that you stated earlier, and that have to do with the information that you obtained from your wife. You told, during chief examination, that your wife went to Odzak and was told there that everything was done in order to facilitate your exchange and that as a result of that she was taken to the room where she could overhear the conversation to that effect. After your exchange, meaning after the 4th of July, 1992, you heard all this from your wife; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife happen to tell you when did this event take place when she was taken to the room to hear the conversation in Odzak? Did she tell you when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to her, and now that I'm able to analyse all of these events, it could have been somewhere before the 24th or 25th, because between the 24th and 26th of May, the four of us were brought from Serbia in order to be exchanged. That's what we were told, at least. Since the exchange did not take place until the beginning of July, I suppose that it could have been, as I've just told you, at the end of May. My wife at the time was told that we were in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife tell you something about who was present in that room in Odzak and between whom did the conversation take place? Or rather, who was the person on the Samac side taking part in the conversation? Did your wife tell you about these persons? Did your wife know these persons or do you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: She told me about one person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Gujic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the name is with K, for the G. Here in the transcript is says G, G-i-c. It's with K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How do you spell it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. K-u-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it just that person, Mr. Kujic present there, or were there some other persons present during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go into great detail with her regarding that. I don't like going back to that. All she told me was that she went on a number of occasions, that she sought this on a number of occasions too, and on that occasion Kujic permitted her to be present when that conversation about the exchange took place. So this was done in order to convince her that they didn't want to exchange me and that they asked for two pilots in exchange for me. Later on I inquired around about whether these pilots really existed, and I was told that they never existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question regarding Mr. Kujic, whom you have mentioned. Can you tell us where does he hail from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him before. Now I know that he lives in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how come he was in Odzak and took place in these negotiations, if he was originally from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you understood the witness's answer, he said he didn't know him before. Later on he came to know that he's from Croatia, not that he was living -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would like now to focus on the very day of your exchange. Let me just ask you one more thing regarding this. You have already stated here that your wife used to work and that she had been hired by Mr. Zaric and that she had known him for many years. I even have some information indicating that you, your wife, Mr. Zaric, and his wife vacationed together several times and that you have a lot in common. So isn't it unusual, then, that your wife, who knows Mr. Zaric very well, did not go to see him and ask him whether he could help you regarding her husband? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, that's first of all inviting him to speculate on his wife's motivations; and secondly, I don't know if Mr. Lazarevic recalls, but he said in evidence that his wife left on the 16th of April and was in Croatian-held territory throughout the period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- throughout the period of time until his exchange. I'm pretty sure that was his evidence in chief. So I don't know if -- unless I'm mistaken, I don't know if Mr. Lazarevic is expecting that she would have crossed enemy lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about her presence in Odzak and this whole episode took place in Odzak. This is the way I understood. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. I don't think there's any question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So this is not Croatia. This is still Bosnia-Herzegovina. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Yes. Yes. It may well be. But I understood it was held by Croatian forces, unless I'm wrong. I mean, there's been evidence in the fall of Odzak, and she was in areas controlled by Croatian forces that may have been Bosnia-Herzegovina. But the question is why didn't she go and see Zaric, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Only the wife can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. I apologise. I -- first of all, my question was not why she didn't went to see Mr. Zaric, why she didn't speak with Mr. Zaric when she already heard him -- MR. DI FAZIO: On the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the radio, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: My apologies. I misunderstood, then. I thought counsel was asking this witness why his wife didn't go into Serb-controlled Bosanski Samac and speak to Mr. Zaric. I thought that was a bit unrealistic, but I apologise. I misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, anyway, that question of mine was a bit speculative regarding this witness. But maybe he spoke with his wife and maybe he asked her, "Why didn't you do that?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, maybe, because only the wife who was present could answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How much more time, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 10 to 15 minutes, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you perhaps ask your wife about the situation when this happened, did you ask her, "Why didn't you talk to Zaric and tell him to do something to have you transferred to the other side"? Did you speak about this topic with her at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife told me that she had been allowed to get in and to hear the negotiations, and they had told her -- they indicated with the gesture with their fingers that she would keep quiet, and she had heard the whole conversation. Then they told her, "See, you can't say that we are not asking for him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another thing that I wanted to note regarding what Mr. Lazarevic has just said: It is correct that we were on good terms, that my relationship with Mr. Zaric in private life was a good one up until 1992. I would also like to note that my wife, while the phones were still in working order, in April, she called all the neighbours that lived near us. She called the police because she knew some of them. And let me give you an example. Mihaljo Topolovac told her, "Everything's fine. Your husband will be here. Nobody's touched him. He will be interrogated, and if he has no blame, if he's not guilty of anything, he will come home." Everybody that she got in touch with told her the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would now like to go through the day of your actual exchange. You told us here already that you were taken from the police station and that you were among the first ones to get on the bus in front of the school and that then you had to wait for the bus to be filled with all the other people that were to be exchanged. Do you remember an incident that occurred at that time, when the police officers from Gorica came, and that they wanted to get you off the bus? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You entered the bus in front of the high school building; that was the incident that I want to talk about now. That's the first incident. So you are already on the bus, and several police officers came from Gorica. They saw you and wanted to get you off the bus, because they didn't want to allow you to be exchanged and they wanted to keep you there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: When I was brought to Samac, when I was put on the bus, I didn't look left or right. I just stood there and I could hardly wait for the bus to be filled with people and for us to leave. Believe me, I don't really remember that, the events in Samac. As regards Samac, in fact, I remember some other incidents, but I don't remember this one in Samac. I really don't. That's the first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, I cannot insist on you answering about things that you don't remember, but I want to know whether you remember an incident that occurred in Lipovac, when some soldiers from Vukovar also wanted to board the bus and to take you out of the bus, you personally, and to do something to you. I wouldn't want to speculate what they wanted to do, but at any rate, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that Zaric stood between you and those people, and not only him, but some other people from Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember just that on the 5th of July -- we were brought there on the 4th -- when we were supposed to go for the exchange from the stop, some people came there and walked around the bus and came to the window where I was sitting, knocking on the pane, jumping onto the bus. I was sitting next to a man, whose full name I remember, and he told me, "Let's change seats." And I said, "No, no. I'd rather remain where I am." I was sitting in the middle of the bus. I remember that I was sitting on the left-hand side. That was the side where the driver's seat is. There was some kind of a ruckus there at the entry to the bus. Some people were not allowed to get in. I don't know who was there, but I do know that they wanted to take me out of the bus. But the security that was there would not allow them to take me out of the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender two documents into evidence. These are lists of exchanged persons for July 4th, 1992. First list is a list of exchanged women and children. This is the document that we received from the Office of the Prosecution. We have official translation. And I would like the witness to take a look at the document regarding certain names that are on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. MR. DI FAZIO: Does the document have an ERN number, I wonder?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. 00734763. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I already gave a copy to our colleagues from the Prosecution. It was yesterday, so they do have this. Their document. We received it from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is the document that we received from the Prosecution. If you could perhaps put the B/C/S version on the ELMO. The two versions are exactly, in fact, the same, because it's just a list of names, but this would allow the defendants to follow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the letters are rather small, so I don't see it will be quite legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you can magnify a bit this document, because the witness is complaining about letters that are very small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can direct the witness to the numbers of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will direct the witness to the numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, sir, I think that now we can read it quite clearly on our screens. The person listed under 9, you will agree with me that it says here Cvitkusic, Ljuba.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know this person, personally? Her nickname is Ljupka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that this is the daughter of Ivana Prgomet, perhaps now this would remind you. It would be easier for you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, Cvitkusic would then be her married name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was her married name? Prgomet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know her, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I can now tell who the person would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now we have under 10, Matic Adila, and it says plus 2. This means, or at least according to the practice that we've seen here at the Tribunal, this would mean that she had two children with her. Do you know Adila Matic? She is the wife of Ante Matic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Ante Matic. I don't know who Anto Matic would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's Djuro Prgomet's cousin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Nephew.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if she is from Samac, could you please tell me who she is, because this last name, Matic, it's a Croatian last name, and Adila, judging from her first name, I would say she is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Here we have the next person, Mara Matic. She is Djuro Prgomet's sister, married to a man by the name of Matic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the name, but I don't know her. I don't know these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 13, we have Snjezana Prgomet. Do you know her, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the name Snjezana rings a bell, but now if you could just remind me. This name Prgomet is probably her married name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Mario Prgomet's sister. So that would not be her married name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: So she is still unmarried?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And here we have also Mara Prgomet, under number 14. Do you know her? She is Djuro Prgomet's wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know quite a few people, but I'm really sorry. Perhaps I do know Djuro, I don't remember Mara any more. But I know approximately where their house is, and I guess that these would be the people that I'm thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what are you trying to establish on this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will get to my point in this second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because we are not getting anywhere with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we will get in a second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said that you knew Djuro Prgomet, and all the people here are women of Croatian ethnic origin related to Djuro Prgomet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are named Prgomet, but I don't know if they're related to him. Now, you are saying how they are related to him, but I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because of the following fact: All these persons are related to Zaric, whose daughter, Natasa Prgomet was married to a member of that family. That was her father-in-law, his brother, his wife, sister-in-law, and their two children. Do you now remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, but I don't -- I can't recall the image now, but I do know that she was married to that family, to the family of Djuro Prgomet. I think they lived in Samac, in Pionirska Street, near Mebos. I know approximately where the house was. I know Djuro, but I don't remember these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had in mind to tender one more document. It is related to the men that were exchanged on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So let's have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In this situation, I really don't feel I should do that maybe. But if the witness can only confirm if some of the persons were exchanged together with him, I don't need to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't you just ask him by narrating the names, if he can remember them? Can we have this one marked for identification only, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I can only have the number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked as D30/4 for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the Serbo-Croat one will be D30/4 ter. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not certain if we need an ID number for this document, because we received it from the Prosecution, and I don't believe that they will have any objection regarding this document, and particularly since I know that this document will be used again by Mr. Lukic in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The problem is that the questions you put to the witness regarding the contents of these documents, he doesn't know any of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I don't want to insist on this. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when were you exchanged? Or rather, when you were exchanged, were Djuro Prgomet, Prgomet Marko, and Ivo Cvitkusic with you? Do you know these three people, and were they with you when you were exchanged, and were they exchanged with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we who were exchanged, we set off on the 4th, but we were in fact exchanged on the 5th, between 12.00 and 1.00, and I saw a list here when I was here the last time. There were about 40-odd of us who were on the bus. And I think that the persons that you mentioned, I don't remember whether they were with me on the bus, because there were five buses. And let me just mention in this regard that when we were exchanged, when we were brought to the line of exchange, when we came there from the direction of Serbia, my bus was the first, and there was a roll-call. On the other side, from the Croatian side, a bus came in. I don't know how many people were there. I only know that our names were read out on our side. I suppose that the same thing happened for the first bus there, to verify who was there, and the other buses that had come in, they just got off and moved onto another bus on the other side, and their names were not called out. I don't have any doubts about the fact that these people were exchanged, but I really don't remember that they were with me on the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please confirm for me that these people were related to Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons by the name of Prgomet were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. We have three minutes to go before the break, because we are expecting to start the other witness at 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you perhaps think, Your Honours, that it would be wise for me to start my cross-examination right now? As far as I'm concerned, I can do it, but I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can start. Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir, Witness A. I will not repeat the same things that my colleague already told you about the way in which the examination will go on. I am Novak Lukic and I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Tadic, and I will be conducting this cross-examination on his behalf. I will try to ask questions in such a way that they are very short and clear, to elicit very precise answers. If you have the information, then please answer with my question, preferably, with yes or no. If you don't remember or if you don't know, please say so. In the few minutes that we have, I will make a brief introduction through my questions. You first spoke with the investigators from the OTP in 1994. That's what you said to my colleague Mr. Lazarevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you spoke with the Prosecutors in 2001, in June. Do you remember that? This conversation took place in Odzak, as far as the Prosecutors informed us. Do you remember that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke with the Prosecutors in June this year. Do you remember how long this interview took in June this year, when you spoke to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how long it took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have our break, and we'll continue with Witness A tomorrow at 1415 hours. We shall continue our proceedings at 1600 hours with the other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. Before we proceed, yesterday I had indicated to the legal officer that the Prosecution witnesses, the Bobics, could be released, because it won't be possible to hear them this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're going to e-mail our counterparts back at the office and notify them to release them immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're having a problem with the video. All right. Thank you. Examined by Mr. Weiner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Subasic.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we talked about a couple of matters. We talked about several matters, and I would just like to clarify two before we move on. Yesterday we discussed visits to the primary school by Miroslav Tadic to read the persons' names who were to be exchanged. And I asked you if you were certain as to the number of visits, and you indicated no, you didn't know the number. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Although you don't know the exact number, are we speaking of one visit, two visits, or several visits that Miroslav Tadic made to the school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several visits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Miroslav Tadic visited the primary school in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I would read this line to you, tell me if this refreshes your recollection, on page 4 of the 1998 interview: "Sometime during mid-June 1992, Miroslav Tadic came to the primary school. He came into the gym where we were detained. Tadic came together with some people from the Serbian Red Cross in Bosanski Samac." Does that refresh your recollection at all, sir, as to whether or not Miroslav Tadic visited in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what I stated then, that he had come in June, then he must have. A long time has passed since the moment when I gave that statement. It's been four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you recall during the summer period he came several times?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, sir, we also had some discussion about your going back to the Territorial Defence building, also referred to as the TO, at the end of the summer, sometime in late August. Now, that was your -- according to your second detention there. When did you see Dr. Blagoje Simic, when you were detained that second time at the TO or at the time of your first detention at the TO in April? When did you see Dr. Blagoje Simic at the TO?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you see him in the TO facility, in what part of the facility?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the courtyard of the TO building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long was he there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. Perhaps some five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in November of 1992, while you were being held at the TO, did something happen? Were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In late November of 1992, we were transferred to the Batkovici camp, near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "we," about how many -- first, when you say "we," do you mean other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the prisoners from Samac were transferred to the camp in Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that point, you had been in various camps in Samac from May of 1992 through November of that same year?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were at those prison camps in Bosanski Samac, were you able to bathe or take a shower?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to wash your clothes?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given sufficient bandages or medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's continue with the conditions at those camps. Let's talk about the food that you were given. How many meals did you receive each day at those various camps in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court here what that meal consisted of?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would divide one loaf of bread among 16 to 18 people. In the beginning, we would receive some marmalade to put on the bread and some tea, and later on they would give us lard to spread on the bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what is lard?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it comes from pig fat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are Muslims allowed to eat lard or this product from pig fat?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the prisoners want to eat the lard?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They naturally did not want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards ever say anything to the prisoners when they received lard for their bread?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would laugh. They would use derogatory terms and say things like, "Well, look at them. They can eat it now," and say things along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What derogatory things did they say to the Muslims in relation to them receiving lard with their meal?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would say, "Look at balijas eating pork," and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these portions that you received of bread and tea, was that sufficient, enough of a meal for you or the other men?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you before, they would divide one loaf of bread between 16 to 18 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question: Was that a sufficient amount of food for you, that one slice of bread or however much bread you had? Was that a sufficient amount of bread for you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how could it have been sufficient?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, with that one meal a day, were you or the other prisoners hungry?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were, all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you feel weak from the lack of food?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose any weight? Did you or any -- start off with you yourself. Did you lose any weight?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, about 25 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that you lost 25 kilogrammes?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to the Batkovici camp, then in December the Red Cross came and registered us, and then they weighed us, gave us some clothing, and this is how I learned how much I weighed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only prisoner who lost weight or did any of the other prisoners lose a significant amount of weight?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody had lost weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we leave this topic of food at the camps in Bosanski Samac, who was responsible for bringing the food to the various prison camps in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name of that person, but I know that he was the brother of Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you went to Batkovici. At Batkovici, were the conditions better? Worse? The same? How were the conditions at that camp?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were better than in Samac, but they were far from good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how many meals were you given a day in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, we would receive three meals, and later on, two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there regular beatings at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there beatings at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these severe beatings?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were prisoners able to bathe at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why the conditions at Batkovici were better than those at Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the camp was registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's discuss this matter: Do you know whether the local community was involved in the operation of the camp at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of the guards watching us there were from the Batkovici local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you get a chance to speak with some of those guards from the local commune at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you the role that the local community played at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that on one occasion they put up barricades. It was at the time when the camp had already been opened. They said that they did not want to bring a bad name to their village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they tell you what the result was of their protest of barricades against having an infamous camp in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The result was that they were employed as guards. They also invited the Red Cross over, the camp was registered, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having local persons serve as guards, were there any severe beatings by the guards as those that you had at the TO or the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did these local guards allow the paramilitaries to enter and beat and torture the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that while at Batkovici, the Red Cross, the International Red Cross -- or the camp was registered with the International Red Cross. Did the Red Cross ever visit -- and I mean the International Red Cross -- ever visit the prisoners, including yourself, while at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, approximately every other week or once a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time that you saw or met with the International Red Cross at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in early December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you met them at that time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all registered. We were given new clothing, we were weighed, we were sprayed against fleas, we were given some food, canned food, and I think we also got some cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of being registered with the Red Cross and their visits, were you able to send and receive mail?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to send mail through the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were detained at Batkovici, did you ever send or receive mail? Did you ever send or receive mail to members of your family?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on a number of occasions. I both sent mail and received it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any conversation -- did you or the other prisoners have any conversation with members of the Red Cross concerning the prison camps in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We talked to them on several occasions, and we told them about the camp in Zasavica, near Samac. We asked them to go and register that camp in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if anything happened as a result of your conversations with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later learn that the Red Cross did check on the camp in Zasavica? Did you ever learn whether they did that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. [Interpretation] The previous question: Do you know if anything happened as a result of your conversations? The witness said, on line -- on page 37, line 25, the witness replied that he didn't know, and now the Prosecutor repeated the question, even though the witness had already answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just trying to refresh the witness's recollection. I can read a sentence from his -- from the Prosecutor's notes on pages 4 and 5, where he indicates that they had later learned that the Red Cross had inquired and had put pressures on the authorities to check on the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What statement is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That is the most recent -- the most recent notes or the most recent interview with the witness of last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against this being pointed out to the witness, like we did yesterday, but I object to these questions which already contain the answer and therefore are leading questions. This previous question, in view of the fact that we had already had the answer, in which the witness said he didn't know, is just not clear to me. There is no need to put these types of questions. This is not a statement of the witness; these are Prosecutor's notes, and I think the Prosecutor should point that out, that he's quoting from the Prosecutor's notes, not from the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I just did that. I said these are the notes from the interview of last week. All I want to do is see if I can refresh his recollection. It's not a major point. If you'd like me to move on, I'll move on, but you can use any sort of document, ranging from a piece of paper to, in law school they teach you, a banana to refresh a witness's recollection. Any type of document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Weiner. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you visit with the Red Cross while at Batkovici? An exact number isn't required. Just a few? Several? Many? Once?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Batkovici camp, I spent some 22 months. The Red Cross came twice a week, sometimes once a month, so you can count how many times it was: Over 20 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, while you were at Batkovici, were you required to perform any type of labour?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We worked every day, various tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said you worked every day, did you work within the prison camp at Batkovici or outside of it?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of jobs did you have to perform outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Digging trenches, loading, unloading. We worked in the Zitopromet company. On one occasion, they hired us out to work in the Bijeljina prison -- in fact, to work for the Bijeljina prison, a prison in a mill. Then we strung out the high-tension lines from Ugljevik, from the Ugljevik electrical plant, coal-fired electrical plant, power plant, to another place, and then we also worked on a farm. We also worked in the fields in Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said -- you indicated that you were hired out. By being hired out, were you and the other prisoners paid for this work?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not paid. Those people who hired us out were paid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you dug trenches. Where did you dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Teocak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that in relation to the battle lines?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the area that you dug trenches, were there any troops?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, it's not a classical form of objection, but I just wonder where we are going with this line of questioning. Batkovici camp doesn't have any relevance to the Samac case. People who are running Batkovici camp are by any -- there's not any relation with the defendants in this case. So I would kindly ask to hear the explanation from the Prosecution; otherwise, my objection is based on the irrelevance with our particular case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to cover this issue briefly and have the witness discuss on one occasion, when the prisoners were taken out, 16 to 17 prisoners were in fact killed during an attack, and this witness had to identify those prisoners to see which ones came from Bosanski Samac. He identified the bodies. Now, the reason that I'm trying to introduce this is for three reasons: One, we have to prove, under Article 5, that the crimes committed were widespread and systematic. Having the prisoners dig, not only in Bosanski Samac, outside of Bosanski Samac, having them dig trenches from various camps, proves the widespread and systematic nature of the use of prisoners and civilians for trench-digging in very dangerous situations. Number two, we've had some testimony as to the proof of dangerousness of trench digging, how people were killed, how people were shot. And number three, just the dangerousness that they did not have any barriers or any protections for these people and bullets were flying over their heads. This is further proof or circumstantial proof of the dangerous of trench digging. That's why it's considered inhumane conduct in violation of the various conventions. And finally, number three, it's evidence of a consistent pattern of conduct under Rule 93. The use of forced labour in dangerous conditions was almost a general policy or a modus operandi of the various Serb authorities within the area surrounding Bosanski Samac. And pursuant to the Kvocka decision, what I'd like to do is show it as a consistent pattern of conduct that was perpetrated by the authorities in that area upon those prisoners and villagers, and I'd argue, for those three reasons, this evidence is admissible, and I only want to spend a few minutes on the issue anyway. But I'd argue that it is, in fact, admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, you should go to those points, salient points, as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that -- you indicated that you were on the front lines digging those trenches. Do you recall a situation while you were at Batkovici where a number of people were killed or injured in the process of digging trenches along those front lines? Could you tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period between 1993 and 1994, 16 to 17 people were killed. I remember that it was wintertime and that people were taken at dawn to dig trenches. It was still dark at that time, and they were killed en route. I know that because I went there to identify a lad from Bosanski Samac, so I saw the dead people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were they killed, sir?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on a truck, shot in a truck, and I think that on that occasion our units carried out an incursion into the rear. I mean, the BH army units carried out an incursion into the rear of the Serbian army, and they thought that these were soldiers going out to relieve another unit, so they killed them by mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I was wondering, because the witness said it was between 1993 and 1994, and yet the indictment only goes up to 1993, December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. For the same issue, under the Kvocka decision where they had matters which were not listed in the indictment, and they used it as circumstantial proof, once again, not as direct proof against the defendants but as circumstantial proof to establish certain matters within the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you brought, sir -- while you were at Batkovici, were you brought to -- were you brought somewhere for some sort of trial?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken to the Bijeljina court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What I'm going to do is read a statement from your 1998 statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. We'll move things along on the trial, and I'll ask you a few questions concerning the attorneys and the trial itself after that. But to move things along, let me just read the statement and ask you whether or not this is what occurred: "In the summer of 1993, I was brought to Bijeljina for a trial at the military court. In Bijeljina, I had to give a statement to an investigative judge. I was asked about weapons, whether I had killed somebody, and if I was or had ever been a member of the SDA. After answering these questions, I was taken back to Batkovici. A few days later, some military policemen came with my statement. That statement was totally different from what I had given them. The facts had been twisted and changed. After a few days, I was taken back to Bijeljina for sentencing. I had a lawyer, but in my opinion, this lawyer was even worse than the judge. He did not do anything to help me. I was sentenced to 12 years. After sentencing, I was again taken back to Batkovici." Sir, is that a fair and accurate statement as concerns what happened to you in Bijeljina in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few questions concerning your legal representation or the lack thereof. Were you able to meet with your lawyer prior to questioning?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your lawyer ever advise you as to the legal issues involved?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever speak to you about the nature of the charges?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever discuss with you any possible defences or potential witnesses?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your lawyer ever consult with you during questioning?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about after questioning?

utterances.speaker: HASAN SUBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. He was there just for the appearance's sake.
